profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a civilian sport psychology researcher and an Army training modernization officer to design a 6-week pilot at Fort Moore that adapts sport-based perceptual-cognitive decision drills for a platoon leader course. The agenda is to decide how the pilot will fit into the existing course calendar, what materials and assessments will be used, who owns setup and delivery tasks, and what evidence will be presented to leadership afterward. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the pilot schedule, responsibilities, and a brief for the course commander on what will be implemented.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Associate Professor of Sport Psychology and Director of the Applied Decision Lab
members.expertise: Perceptual-cognitive training, video-occlusion methods, expert performance research, transfer evaluation
members.background: She has spent a decade designing decision-training interventions for elite soccer and rugby academies and recently joined a defense-funded collaboration on adapting high-performance training methods for tactical settings.
members.private_state: She wants the military collaboration to produce a publishable feasibility study and a strong basis for a larger grant, so she is quietly trying to preserve standardized delivery, measurable pre/post data, and enough methodological rigor to claim evidence-based impact.
hidden_assumptions: A pilot is still a research-quality feasibility study with consent procedures, standardized sessions, and analyzable pre/post measures.
Baseline means a custom pre-intervention assessment using her lab's laptop-based video-occlusion task administered individually.
A debrief or AAR should include immediate individual reflection on perceived cues before any group discussion begins.
If the program works, there should be measurable near-transfer gains on the decision task plus acceptable attendance and adherence.
Once a course lead says yes, quiet testing space and short protected assessment windows are normally available.

members.name: Major Evan Cole
members.expertise: Infantry training integration, course scheduling, doctrine implementation, field exercise design
members.background: He previously served as a company commander and observer-controller and now helps the brigade introduce new training methods that commanders will accept without increasing schedule friction or administrative burden.
members.private_state: He wants something the commander can approve quickly and instructors can absorb with minimal disruption, and he is quietly avoiding anything that sounds like a formal research protocol that could slow approval or take extra student time.
hidden_assumptions: A pilot means a limited trial insertion into one existing course cycle under normal training authority, not a formal study.
Baseline means the course's existing reception-week tactical decision exercise scores, which are already documented.
A debrief or AAR refers to the standard instructor-led collective review at the end of the training block.
If the program works, cadre should be able to run it with current staffing and commanders should see obvious relevance during field lanes.
Using the existing course calendar means any added activity must fit inside current blocks rather than require separate testing appointments.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to run a 'pilot' before wider adoption.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a structured feasibility study with standardized delivery, dedicated assessments, and documentation suitable for evidence claims.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a low-friction trial insertion into one course cycle to see if commanders and instructors tolerate it operationally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word pilot is common in both research and military training contexts and sounds perfectly aligned at planning level, so each hears their own familiar default without feeling any need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to getting a 'baseline' in week one.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of her lab's custom pre-test: a laptop-based video-occlusion assessment administered individually before trainees receive any intervention.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the course's existing reception-week tactical decision exercise scores that instructors already collect as part of normal training.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Baseline sounds like a routine planning shorthand rather than a point needing negotiation, and both assume there is an obvious pre-existing default assessment for the other person as well.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree each session will have a short 'AAR' or 'debrief.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a structured immediate reflection process in which each trainee records the cues they noticed and the moment they committed to a decision before group discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the standard instructor-led collective after-action review already used in the course, focused on what happened and what the squad or platoon should do next time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: AAR and debrief feel like near-equivalents across domains, and both versions are plausible enough that surface agreement appears complete even though the method and data generated would differ substantially.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the pilot 'works' and is ready to 'scale.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks it works if trainees show measurable improvement on the decision task and the intervention can be described as evidence-based for a larger rollout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks it works if cadre can deliver it with existing manpower, students do not lose key field time, and leadership sees practical value during lanes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both parties sincerely want the program to succeed and use the same positive language, but the threshold for success sits in different institutional logics that rarely get articulated in an initial planning conversation.

turns.inner_thought: If we can get a clean six-week feasibility study into the next course cycle, I can show this approach travels beyond sport. I need standardized delivery, attendance tracked, and enough structure that the pilot yields publishable pre/post evidence rather than just anecdotes. At this stage, 'pilot' should be easy for him to endorse.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Major. What I'd like to do today is map out a six-week pilot for the next platoon leader course cycle and make sure the sport-based decision drills translate cleanly into your training context.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she's saying pilot, not study. If we keep this as a limited trial inside one course cycle, the commander will listen. The main thing is no extra bureaucracy, no separate approvals that stall us, and something we can scale only if it proves workable to cadre and visible in the field.
turns.utterance: That lines up with what the commander wants. He'd like something practical that fits the current calendar, and if the pilot lands well, we can talk about how it might scale.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep the structure simple so he doesn't balk: week-one baseline on the laptop task, then two brief standardized interventions each week, then a post measure late in the cycle. If I can preserve the sequence, I can at least estimate feasibility and near-transfer.
turns.utterance: Great. My first pass would be a six-week sequence: get a baseline in week one, run two short decision-training inserts per week, and then do a post measure near the end.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. If baseline just means the reception-week decision event they already do, then we've avoided adding student admin time right out of the gate. That's exactly the kind of low-friction start I can defend.
turns.utterance: I think the baseline piece should be pretty easy. In reception week we already collect decision data, so we should be able to use that without adding extra student admin time.

turns.inner_thought: He seems comfortable with baseline, good. On delivery, my lab can own the stimulus prep. I also need each insert to include immediate written reflection before any social contamination from group discussion. I'll call it a short AAR so it sounds familiar.
turns.utterance: That helps. On our side, the lab can prepare the occlusion clips and session materials. I'd also like each insert to end with a short AAR, just to capture what they noticed before discussion.

turns.inner_thought: No issue there. Cadre already run AARs at the end of training blocks, so this can ride inside the normal rhythm rather than becoming a separate event. As long as she isn't asking for extra manpower, we should be fine.
turns.utterance: The AAR piece should be straightforward. The cadre already do end-of-block AARs, so they can absorb that into the normal flow.

turns.inner_thought: I need to secure the logistics now before the calendar hardens. For the baseline and post, I need protected, quiet assessment windows and a room where trainees can complete the laptop task individually without interruption. If I don't ask directly, the data quality will be compromised.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want to flag early is space and timing. For the baseline and the post sessions, it would really help to have a quiet room and short protected windows so the pilot data stay clean enough to interpret.

turns.inner_thought: I can probably carve out short inserts during existing blocks, but separate appointments outside the course flow are where this gets hard. If instructors feel this creates drag, the pilot won't survive, no matter how interesting the concept is. For me, it has to work operationally as well as conceptually.
turns.utterance: I can work on reserving short course inserts, but anything beyond the normal training blocks will be harder to justify unless the pilot clearly works for instructors too.

turns.inner_thought: That's fair, but if the effect is there and adherence is solid, we should have enough evidence to support a broader rollout and a stronger funding case. I need him thinking ahead to January companies as the next sample, assuming the measures behave.
turns.utterance: Understood. My thought is that if the pilot works, we should have enough evidence to recommend a broader package for the January companies.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned: keep it light, use the baseline we've already got, let cadre handle the AARs in stride, and brief leadership on a manageable trial that can scale if it proves useful in practice. I can sell that without creating resistance.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll brief the commander that we're looking at a low-friction pilot in the next cycle, built into the existing calendar, using the baseline from week one and the normal AAR structure, with a recommendation on scale if it works.
